comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological quality and study design (C1, C76-C87). Both evaluations praise the high-quality sEEG data, extensive cortical coverage, large patient sample, and ecological validity of continuous stimuli. OpenEval notes internal consistency and proper ethical approval; peer reviewers emphasize spatial/temporal resolution and generalizability.

Complete agreement on preprocessing methods (C88-C92). Both evaluations affirm the appropriateness and rigor of standard preprocessing procedures, artifact rejection, and frequency band selection. Peer reviewers specifically praise permutation approaches and cross-validation/regularization.

Strong agreement on shared neural responses (C2, C16-C20, C22). Both evaluations support the core finding that speech and music largely share network-level brain activities. OpenEval emphasizes convergence across spectral power and connectivity analyses; peer reviewers provide explicit affirmation from all three reviewers. OpenEval also includes C23-C24 and C40-C43, C69 which peer R1 addresses partially (C23-C24) and peer R5 addresses partially (C40-C43).

Significant disagreement on anatomical selectivity claims (C3, C48, C49, C56, C72). OpenEval finds these claims fully supported by population prevalence analyses. However, peer reviewers rate this as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about theoretical accuracy of selectivity concept, spatial resolution limitations (electrodes record from thousands of neurons), and potential for microscale selectivity being masked.

Strong agreement on frequency-specific selectivity (C4, C25-C27, C44-C47, C62, C73). Both evaluations support that selectivity exists at the level of frequency-specific distributed networks rather than anatomical regions. Peer reviewers praise the comprehensive spectral analysis and acknowledge heterogeneity across frequency bands as a key strength. OpenEval also includes C57 which peer R6 addresses.

Complete agreement on TRF encoding findings (C28-C37, C65-C68). Both evaluations support that low-frequency activity better encodes acoustic features than high-frequency amplitude. Peer reviewers acknowledge the encoding models and temporal response functions as well-presented and straightforward, with no challenges to the quantitative findings.

Complete agreement on connectivity findings (C38-C39). Both evaluations support the seed-based connectivity analysis showing quantitative differences across frequency bands. OpenEval addresses C38-C39 specifically; peer R5 addresses these plus C40-C43 (which OpenEval R2 also covers), affirming low selectivity across spectral signatures in connectivity measures.

Partial disagreement on conceptual framework (C58, C70-C71, C74-C75). OpenEval finds the tripartite classification (shared/preferred/selective) well-supported and valuable. Peer reviewers are UNCERTAIN: one praises it as a 'welcome lens,' but others critique it as resembling traditional ANOVA, potentially oversimplified, and not fully capturing complexity. Suggestion for continuous metrics instead of categorical approach.

Agreement on methodological limitations (C61, C64, C63). Both evaluations acknowledge that the temporal integration approach cannot isolate specific operations and may overlook intricate details in neural coding. OpenEval praises the authors' scientific rigor in acknowledging this; peer reviewers explicitly note the study doesn't differentiate diverse content within speech/music or delve into functional mechanisms.

Agreement on complementary frequency patterns (C23-C24). OpenEval finds these claims supported by Figures 2 and 3, describing frequency-specific patterns. Peer R1 includes these claims in their broader affirmation of shared neural responses, though doesn't specifically discuss the complementary pattern observation.

OpenEval acknowledges sampling bias (C21) and finds the authors appropriately cautious, with evidence that patterns remain similar across hemispheres. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this limitation.

OpenEval finds literature review claims (C5-C15, C50-C55, C59-C60, C63) well-supported with appropriate citations and fair characterization of mixed evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the literature review, though peer R7 touches on C63 regarding limitations.
